newsitem.title: USA: U.S. unlikely to send troops to Zaire - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. unlikely to send troops to Zaire - Pentagon.

text.p: The United States has tentatively decided not to send troops to Zaire and will instead provide military cargo planes to help fly humanitarian aid to the refugees streaming home to Rwanda, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.

"At one point, it looked like we needed a security component" to protect the distribution of aid to refugees in Goma, Zaire, Defense Department spokesman Ken Bacon told Reuters. "Now it looks like we won't need a security component."

Instead, Bacon said, the U.S. military is already moving to set up an air bridge to Kigali in Rwanda and will help fly in food and other supplies for distribution within Rwanda by the United Nations and other aid groups. U.S. Air Force teams were already being moved to Entebbe, Uganda, and Kigali to set up a relay, he said.

"We will concentrate on getting supplies to refugees in Rwanda now and, if necessary later, in Zaire," Bacon said in response to questions about a Washington Post report that senior U.S. officials had tentatively concluded that an earlier-planned military security operation led by Canada was unnecessary.

President Bill Clinton agreed last week to send about 1,000 U.S. troops to Goma as part of an international military force under U.N. auspices. The American troops were to help secure the Goma airport and set up a safe corridor for refugees to return to nearby Rwanda.

But Bacon said on Tuesday that the movement of tens of thousands of refugees back to Rwanda in recent days had sharply reduced -- and probably ended -- the need for an armed security force and that the United States would instead use several hundred Air Force personnel to help with airlifted aid in Kigali.

While a final decision is expected at a meeting of Canadian, U.S. and other representatives in Stuttgart, Germany, on Thursday, Bacon said the United States was already moving to set up an "aid bridge" with Air Force personnel at Kigali and with a relay point in Entebbe.
Bacon said that the Canadian Army general who had been tapped to lead the security operation was currently in Kigali assessing the situation.

Pentagon officials said on Monday that U.S. Air Force cargo planes and crews had already been moved to Moron Air Base in Spain to take part in a potential airlift operation and that other planes could be moved quickly to countries near Zaire after diplomatic arrangements were made.

The State Department on Monday said a U.S. relief team in Rwanda was working with planners in Washington and U.S. diplomats elsewhere to determine how best to help the refugees, who were streaming back to Rwanda in a 40-mile (64 km) column.
Members of a U.S. Disaster Assistance Team reported that medical supplies were adequate and the World Food Program has more than enough to feed the returning refugees.
